question: Can sequence architectures be decomposed into independently selectable memory structure, internal key-value objective, retention rule, and update algorithm, and do non-Euclidean choices along those axes produce efficient recurrent language models that outperform established transformer and linear-RNN baselines?

key_findings.claim: Miras organizes sequence models around four choices—memory structure, attentional-bias objective, retention gate, and memory-learning algorithm—and connects a cumulative Follow-the-Regularized-Leader view to a one-step learning-retaining view under restricted convex assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 maps attention, Hebbian and delta-rule RNNs, TTT, and Titans into this taxonomy. Proposition 3.2 proves equivalence only when the parameter domain is Euclidean, the cumulative objective plus regularizer is strictly convex, the learning rate is constant, and retention is the specific Bregman divergence generated by that cumulative objective. This is a useful design vocabulary, not a theorem that arbitrary nonconvex deep memories are mutually equivalent.

anchors.section: Table 1 and 3 Associative Memory, Attentional Bias, and Retention

key_findings.claim: The concrete Moneta, Yaad, and Memora variants replace a shallow recurrent state with a two-layer MLP and respectively use an ℓp objective plus ℓq-style retention, a Huber-style switch between ℓ2 and ℓ1 updates, and an ℓ2 objective plus simplex/KL retention.
key_findings.evidence: Equations 24-27 specify the variants, and Figure 2 shows their Llama-like attention-free block and optional sliding-window-attention hybrid. To train the nonlinear recurrences, the implementation described in the paper freezes each token's gradient at the previous chunk boundary, applies nonlinear normalization only between chunks, and treats a boundary token specially for Memora. Thus the scalable training rule is an approximation to, rather than an exact parallel evaluation of, the per-token recurrences used to motivate the models.

anchors.section: 5.3 Miras's Variants: Moneta, Yaad, and Memora
Figure 2 and 5.4 Architecture Backbone and Fast Training

key_findings.claim: The reported language-modeling and commonsense results support competitive Pareto points for the Miras family, but not the prose claim that every variant beats every baseline.
key_findings.evidence: At 340M/15B tokens, Moneta improves WikiText perplexity from the best baseline's 27.01 to 26.19 and Yaad improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.94 to 29.11, yet Yaad's SIQA accuracy is 33.82 versus DeltaNet's 37.96 and its LAMBADA accuracy is 34.09 versus Gated DeltaNet's 34.11. At 1.3B/100B tokens, Moneta reaches 11.47 LAMBADA perplexity versus Gated DeltaNet's 12.17, while its 47.88 LAMBADA accuracy trails the 48.76 hybrid Gated DeltaNet-H2 result and its 61.18 BoolQ score trails Samba's 62.11. Several Miras variants win several columns; none dominates all rows and metrics.

key_findings.claim: On the paper's synthetic single-needle RULER evaluation, all three variants retain substantially more information than the listed recurrent baselines, and the small ablation table is directionally consistent with Yaad's components helping.
key_findings.evidence: Across the nine S-NIAH-PK/N/W cells, Moneta, Yaad, and Memora average 93.5, 92.9, and 92.1 accuracy, versus 75.8 for Gated DeltaNet, 66.1 for TTT, 57.9 for DeltaNet, and 52.0 for Mamba2. Yaad's aggregate LM score is 53.98; removing retention, input-dependent thresholding, one Huber branch, or the MLP reduces it to 50.63-53.04. The paper does not report seed dispersion, uncertainty, or more adversarial multi-query long-context tasks.

key_findings.claim: Several displayed derivations and architecture descriptions are internally inconsistent, so the mathematical specification is not sufficient to reconstruct the evaluated models unambiguously.
key_findings.evidence: For p=1, Equation 12 takes a signed-error outer-product update but does not constrain the memory weights to the claimed two values −1 and +1. The Variant-5 'Bregman divergence' subtracts ⟨W′,W−W′⟩ instead of ⟨∇F(W′),W−W′⟩, although the next update assumes the latter; its sigmoid example also uses Wt rather than Wt−1 inside the right-hand logit. Equation 25 includes ηt inside what is labeled ∇ℓ even though Equation 24 multiplies that gradient by ηt again. Moneta uses q=4 after the motivating ℓq derivation states 1<q≤2, and Memora is introduced as elastic-net retention while its actual update uses KL/simplex retention. The official TeX source additionally contains a duplicated Yaad ℓ2 branch absent from the rendered two-branch equation.

key_findings.claim: The evidence for scale and efficiency is incomplete despite large training runs: the paper reports perplexity-versus-FLOP curves but no measured throughput, latency, memory footprint, uncertainty, or complete reproducibility configuration.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 plots model-size and training-context trends without numerical tables or error bars, and the baselines are imported from Titans rather than documented as fresh matched runs. The appendix lists 170M, 340M, and 780M architectures, while the main text describes 120M, 340M, 760M, and 1.3B models; it omits 1.3B block, width, head, and learning-rate details. Neither the v1 paper nor its official arXiv source links author code, checkpoints, or exact data/evaluation scripts, and Google's later official research post links only the papers.

method.core_idea: Treat a sequence layer as an associative key-value memory whose architecture, inner objective, retention regularizer, and optimizer are separable design axes, then instantiate underexplored robust objectives and non-Euclidean retention rules in deep recurrent memories.
method.mechanism: Input projections produce keys, values, queries, learning rates, retention coefficients, and, for Yaad, Huber thresholds. A two-layer MLP memory is updated online from prediction error and queried recurrently. Moneta changes error and weight geometry with ℓp/ℓq terms, Yaad caps the influence of large errors by switching update form, and Memora projects positive weights onto a simplex using log-space and softmax updates. Chunkwise training replaces within-chunk state-dependent gradients with gradients at a shared boundary state so accelerator-friendly matrix operations can process tokens in parallel.
assumptions: A useful sequence layer can be interpreted as learning an internal key-to-value mapping, even when the original architecture was not derived as an optimizer.
The four proposed choices capture the major causal design differences despite convolutions, projections, normalization, data dependence, and hybrid attention being treated as secondary details.
Stale boundary-state gradients and between-chunk nonlinearities are faithful enough proxies for per-token nonlinear memory updates during large-scale training.
Memora's weights remain strictly positive so logarithms and the KL/simplex update are defined and numerically stable.
Imported baseline results have sufficiently matched token budgets, data, parameter accounting, evaluation harnesses, and optimization to support direct comparisons.

techniques.role: Separates state architecture, write objective, retention geometry, and optimizer to expose a combinatorial sequence-model design space.
Uses ℓp or Huber error geometry to change which key-value mismatches dominate a memory update.
Uses ℓq, KL/simplex, elastic-net, or Bregman-style regularization to change how old state is preserved or removed.
Makes the recurrent state a two-layer MLP whose parameters are updated inside the forward pass.
Freezes gradients at a chunk boundary to turn a nonlinear token recurrence into parallel matrix operations during training.
Varies p, q, retention, threshold dependence, loss branches, and memory depth to test individual framework choices.

evaluations.setting: 340M-parameter models trained on 15B FineWeb-Edu tokens and evaluated on WikiText, LAMBADA, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC, SIQA, and BoolQ.
evaluations.metric: Language-model perplexity and zero-shot task accuracy.
evaluations.result: Miras variants produce the best reported value in several columns—for example Moneta's 26.19 WikiText perplexity versus Gated DeltaNet's 27.01 and Yaad's 39.86 normalized HellaSwag accuracy versus 38.12—but lose other columns, including Yaad's 33.82 SIQA versus DeltaNet's 37.96.
evaluations.baseline: Transformer++, RetNet, GLA, Mamba, DeltaNet, TTT, and Gated DeltaNet, with baseline numbers imported from Titans.

evaluations.setting: 760M/30B-token and 1.3B/100B-token language models, including optional sliding-window-attention hybrids at 760M.
evaluations.metric: The same perplexity and commonsense accuracy suite.
evaluations.result: At 1.3B, Moneta reports 15.52 WikiText and 11.47 LAMBADA perplexity versus Gated DeltaNet's 16.42 and 12.17, while hybrid Gated DeltaNet-H2 remains ahead on LAMBADA accuracy (48.76 versus 47.88) and Samba remains ahead of Moneta on BoolQ (62.11 versus 61.18).
evaluations.baseline: Transformer++, RetNet, Mamba2, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, Samba, and Gated DeltaNet-H2.

evaluations.setting: C4 scaling sweeps over approximately 120M-1.3B parameters and training contexts from 2K to 32K.
evaluations.metric: Perplexity against estimated FLOPs and training-context length.
evaluations.result: The plotted Miras curves are generally below the displayed Transformer, Mamba2, GSA, and TTT curves at the larger settings, but all context-length curves worsen after their mid-range minima and the paper supplies neither raw values nor error bars.
evaluations.baseline: Transformer, Mamba2, GSA, and TTT curves reproduced from the authors' prior experimental framework.

evaluations.setting: RULER single-needle associative retrieval from 1K to 8K context across word, number, and synthetic key-value variants.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy in nine S-NIAH cells and their unweighted average.
evaluations.result: Moneta, Yaad, and Memora average 93.5, 92.9, and 92.1, substantially above Gated DeltaNet at 75.8 and TTT at 66.1.
evaluations.baseline: Mamba2, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and TTT.

evaluations.setting: Moneta p/q sweeps over 2K-16K contexts and component removal from Yaad.
evaluations.metric: Perplexity curves and an aggregate LM score.
evaluations.result: p=3 is best among the displayed p values, q changes the context-length curve, and each listed Yaad removal lowers its 53.98 aggregate score to 50.63-53.04; only point estimates are shown.
evaluations.baseline: Alternative p/q configurations and Yaad without retention, input-dependent thresholding, either loss branch, or deep memory.

limitations: Author-stated: the nonlinear recurrences are slow if evaluated directly, motivating a stale-gradient chunk approximation and delayed nonlinearities rather than exact tokenwise training.
Author-stated: different Miras variants have different strengths, and determining which alternative architecture serves which downstream task is left for future work.

Reviewer inference: Proposition 3.2 covers a strictly convex Euclidean construction and does not establish the paper's broad unification for nonconvex MLP memories, simplex constraints, or the approximated training rules.
Reviewer inference: multiple equations have indexing, gradient, domain, or regularizer inconsistencies that prevent a unique independent implementation from the paper alone.
Reviewer inference: the language-model tables contain no seed-level variance or uncertainty and import baselines from prior work, so small score differences should not be treated as established wins.

Reviewer inference: the efficiency claim is supported by asymptotic reasoning and FLOP plots, not end-to-end throughput, latency, accelerator utilization, activation memory, or inference-cost measurements.
Reviewer inference: the source provides no author implementation or checkpoints, while Table 5 disagrees with the main text's model sizes and omits the 1.3B configuration.
failure_modes: A rare but useful token can look like a Huber outlier, causing Yaad to cap precisely the update that should be memorized.
Large chunks make boundary-state gradients increasingly stale and can train dynamics that differ materially from the tokenwise recurrence used at inference.
Memora can encounter undefined logarithms, underflow, or over-concentrated simplex weights unless strict positivity and stable log-space numerics are enforced.
The ℓq normalization can be ill-conditioned near zero and is ambiguous under the paper's q-domain and exponent inconsistencies.
A single-needle benchmark can be solved by brittle key-value retrieval while multi-hop reasoning, repeated updates, interference, or adversarial distractors still fail.
Fixed-size deep memory can overwrite earlier information as sequence complexity grows even when token count alone is within the demonstrated range.
A framework label may hide important non-factorial interactions among projections, convolutions, normalization, hybrid attention, chunk size, and optimizer settings.
reusable_insights: Treat the write loss and retention geometry as separately ablatable modules rather than baking both into one named recurrence.
When parallel training approximates a sequential learning rule, report both algorithms explicitly and measure their state-trajectory and downstream divergence as chunk size changes.
Robust objectives should be tested on semantically important rare events as well as synthetic noise; reduced outlier influence is not automatically improved memory.
A unifying taxonomy is most valuable when it predicts controlled interventions, so compare models on a factorial grid with matched parameters, tokens, wall-clock compute, and evaluation code.
Long-context validation should jointly measure recall, interference, state tracking, multi-hop reasoning, throughput, and memory usage rather than relying on a single needle score.
Check displayed recurrences with shape, domain, fixed-point, and limiting-case tests before scaling an architecture derived from them.
open_questions: What are the corrected, executable definitions of Moneta and Memora, including the intended q duality, learning-rate placement, and Bregman arguments?
How closely do chunk-trained memory trajectories match exact per-token trajectories, and which discrepancy predicts downstream degradation?
Do non-Euclidean objectives still help under fully matched contemporary Transformer, DeltaProduct, ATLAS, and TTT baselines with confidence intervals?
Which of the four Miras axes has an effect independent of parameter count, projection design, memory depth, and hybrid attention?
Does the memorization interpretation remain operationally useful for Miras variants in light of the 2026 result reducing broad KV-binding TTT classes to learned linear attention?
Can a parallel algorithm preserve the nonlinear recurrence exactly, or can a principled approximation provide a bound connecting training and inference dynamics?
How do these memories behave under conflicting rewrites, distribution shifts, deletion requests, adversarial keys, and continual streams much longer than their training context?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States
competitive_landscape.difference: TTT makes a linear model or two-layer MLP the recurrent hidden state and updates it with a self-supervised loss. Miras abstracts that construction into four design axes and tries robust/non-Euclidean objectives, while inheriting TTT's memory-I/O and chunked-training tension.

competitive_landscape.title: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time
competitive_landscape.difference: Titans supplies the deep test-time MLP memory, surprise-gradient update, momentum, decay, and attention/memory compositions that Miras generalizes. Miras's empirical baseline matrix is largely inherited from Titans, while its three variants emphasize alternative objectives and pure recurrence.

competitive_landscape.title: Test-time regression: a unifying framework for designing sequence models with associative memory
competitive_landscape.difference: Test-time regression derives attention, state-space models, fast weights, and online learners from regression weights, function class, and optimization, and derives higher-order attention. Miras adds retention as an explicit axis and permits non-regression attentional objectives, but its breadth is more interpretive and its nonlinear variants require approximation.

competitive_landscape.title: Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule
competitive_landscape.difference: Gated DeltaNet combines targeted delta updates with rapid gated erasure in a matrix state and has a hardware-oriented parallel algorithm. Miras uses a more expressive deep state and alternative objectives, but provides less direct systems evidence and an approximate nonlinear parallelization.

competitive_landscape.title: DeltaProduct: Improving State-Tracking in Linear RNNs via Householder Products
competitive_landscape.difference: DeltaProduct takes multiple delta steps per token, producing tunable Householder-product transitions with finite-precision state-tracking analysis. Miras exposes optimizer choice as a broader knob and uses deep memories, but its evaluated variants do not provide comparable state-tracking guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: ATLAS: Learning to Optimally Memorize the Context at Test Time
competitive_landscape.difference: ATLAS explicitly targets the online last-token, capacity, and memory-management limits by optimizing memory over current and past tokens and building DeepTransformers. It is a direct continuation that narrows an important failure mode of Miras's one-step variants and reports much longer-context experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: TNT: Improving Chunkwise Training for Test-Time Memorization
competitive_landscape.difference: TNT identifies the chunk-size speed-accuracy conflict left implicit by Miras and decouples it through hierarchical pretraining plus small-chunk fine-tuning, reporting up to 17× speedup. Its premise qualifies Miras's unmeasured claim that chunkwise nonlinear memory is simply fast and parallelizable.

competitive_landscape.title: Nested Learning: The Illusion of Deep Learning Architectures
competitive_landscape.difference: The same authors extend the memory-as-optimization view from sequence layers to nested optimizers, self-modifying update rules, and a continuum memory system. It broadens Miras's taxonomy rather than independently validating its equations or reported model comparisons.

competitive_landscape.title: Test-Time Training with KV Binding Is Secretly Linear Attention
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. show that a broad class of KV-binding TTT layers can be reduced to learned linear attention and report phenomena inconsistent with a literal online-memorization story. The result does not automatically cover every nonlinear Miras variant, but it directly challenges treating the associative-memory interpretation as the unique mechanism.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a general four-choice framework that accurately unifies modern sequence models and uses previously unexplored attentional biases and retention gates to create three fast, parallelizable recurrent models outperforming transformers and linear RNNs.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The framework explicitly separates memory structure, inner objective, retention, and optimizer; the paper instantiates Moneta, Yaad, and Memora at up to 1.3B parameters and reports strong language-model and single-needle results plus limited axis ablations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is the explicit retention axis and the attempt to import robust regression and non-Euclidean online-optimization choices into deep test-time memory. The broad unification overlaps TTT, Titans, and concurrent test-time regression, while several equations are inconsistent and the evaluated recurrence is only approximately trained. Strong point results justify further study, but they do not establish universal dominance, exact equivalence, or systems efficiency. Later ATLAS, TNT, Nested Learning, and the 2026 linear-attention reinterpretation both extend and qualify the original framing.

reviewer_notes: Read every page of the 26-page extracted paper, including all 32 numbered equations, Proposition 3.2 and its proof, all four figures (including the three-panel and two-panel plots), all five tables, the full appendix, and all references. Visual inspection covered the framework diagram, architecture graph, scaling plots, language-model matrix, RULER/ablation results, and architecture-details table. The official v1 arXiv source archive was audited (TeX, bibliography, table include, and nine raster assets); it contains no author code link and exposes additional specification errors, including a duplicated Yaad branch. Google's December 2025 official MIRAS post was also checked and links the papers but no implementation. No training rerun was attempted because no official code/checkpoints are available and the reported experiments require 15B-100B-token runs. Nine primary arXiv competitors/current successors were checked through 2026-08-23. Material contradictions are the invalid ±1-memory inference, malformed Bregman and gradient equations, q/domain and Memora-description mismatches, the prose claim of across-the-board baseline wins despite losing table cells, and inconsistent/omitted architecture specifications.
